records.sourceFile: Effects of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Repeated Sprint Ability - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Wang Y, Su W, Zhang S, Zhao L, Lv Y, Gu B, et al. Effects of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Repeated Sprint Ability: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Nutrients. 2025;17:3475.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies on acute caffeine and repeated sprint ability. Caffeine improved peak power output compared with placebo, with a significant effect at doses of 6 mg/kg or more but not at lower doses, and significant effects within both male and female subgroups.
paper.tldr: Caffeine taken about 60 minutes before testing improved repeated sprint peak power, and the benefit was significant at 6 mg/kg or more but not at 3 to 5 mg/kg. The studies used lab sprint tests with small samples, so match-play effects and side effects were not assessed.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD420251150247) of PubMed, EBSCO, Cochrane Library, Web of Science and Scopus from inception to 6 September 2025, including acute caffeine versus placebo studies with peak power output as the primary outcome. Fastest running sprint times were converted to peak power with a formula, data were pooled as weighted mean differences with fixed-effects models, and subgroups by dose, modality and sex were examined; risk of bias used the Cochrane tool and PEDro, and certainty used GRADE.
paper.findings: Caffeine increased RSA peak power output versus placebo (WMD 5.28, 95% CI 2.49-8.07; p = 0.0002; I2 = 7%). Doses of 6 mg/kg or more gave a significant effect (WMD 6.67, 95% CI 3.32-10.02) and lower doses did not (WMD 2.16, 95% CI -2.87 to 7.19, p = 0.40). Effects were significant within cycling (WMD 8.77) and running (WMD 4.56) protocols and within males (WMD 13.11) and females (WMD 4.03), and the authors rated overall certainty as high.
paper.limitations: Only powder and capsule caffeine were included and not analyzed separately, and training status and habitual caffeine intake were not controlled. The abstract says cycling showed the larger effect (8.77 vs 4.56) while the results and discussion say running did, and no between-subgroup tests are reported for modality or sex, so the 'no significant sex difference' statement is the authors' assertion. The funnel plot showed substantial asymmetry, and adverse effects (higher at 9 mg/kg in one study) were not analyzed.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors recommend 6 mg/kg taken 60 minutes before exercise as an evidence-based strategy for repeated sprint peak power; 9 mg/kg did not add benefit in comparison studies and was linked to more side effects. Lower doses (3 to 5 mg/kg) did not show a significant pooled benefit, though individual studies varied, possibly with habitual caffeine use.
paper.athleteDev: Sports nutrition staff can consider about 6 mg/kg caffeine 60 minutes before repeated sprint work, with attention to individual tolerance and side effects that this review did not assess. The outcome is lab RSA peak power, so transfer to match running still needs checking.
paper.rtp: Not designed for return to sport: included studies tested healthy participants, including some adolescent samples, on RSA performance, so the review cannot inform caffeine use during rehabilitation or after injury.

records.sourceFile: Effect of creatine supplementation on kidney function - a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Naeini EK, Eskandari M, Mortazavi M, Gholaminejad A, Karevan N. Effect of creatine supplementation on kidney function: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Nephrol. 2025;26:622.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 studies on creatine supplementation and kidney function, pooling 12 studies for serum creatinine and 5 for GFR. Creatine produced a small rise in serum creatinine that the authors attribute to creatine turnover, with no significant change in GFR.
paper.tldr: Creatine supplementation slightly raised serum creatinine but did not change GFR in mostly short trials of healthy adults, some athletes and some patients. A higher creatinine in an athlete taking creatine may reflect the supplement rather than kidney damage, and a more specific kidney marker is needed to judge it.
paper.methods: PRISMA review searching PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar (January 2000 to March 2025) for RCTs, non-randomized trials, observational and pre-post studies of oral creatine in humans of any age, sex or health status reporting serum creatinine, GFR or renal outcomes. Risk of bias used RoB 2 for RCTs and Newcastle-Ottawa for other designs; mean differences were pooled with random-effects models in Stata 17, with a creatinine subgroup analysis by follow-up duration and funnel plots, Egger's test and trim-and-fill for publication bias.
paper.findings: Serum creatinine rose slightly with creatine versus control (MD 0.07, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.12, p = 0.03; I2 69.7%), significantly at 1 week or less (MD 0.12, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.21), not at 1 to 12 weeks (MD 0.04, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.17), and again beyond 12 weeks (no estimate printed). Pooled GFR from 5 studies did not differ significantly from control (I2 33.2%). Every study in Table 1 reported no serious adverse effects on the kidney.
paper.limitations: Most studies were short to moderate in duration, data beyond one year are sparse and come from observational cohorts, and dose and training status were too poorly reported for subgroup analysis. Creatinine assays were rarely reported and some are affected by creatine itself, and funnel plots for both outcomes were asymmetric. The text is inconsistent on counts (12 studies, '14 studies' and '16 sets of results' for creatinine), and the creatinine difference is given only in the abstract as 0.07 umol/L with no unit restated in the results.
paper.practicalImplications: For athletes using creatine at standard doses, a small rise in serum creatinine is expected and is not by itself evidence of kidney harm in this review. When kidney function needs checking in an athlete on creatine, the authors advise caution with creatinine-based results and using more specific markers.
paper.athleteDev: Supports the general safety case for creatine in healthy adults at the doses studied (about 5 to 20 g per day, short loading phases), but it reports no performance outcomes. It cannot speak to very long use, very high doses, or athletes with kidney disease.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions: it concerns kidney markers during supplementation, not injury, illness recovery or clearance. It is relevant only when interpreting a raised creatinine in an athlete taking creatine.
